__ year old female with a history of diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease (CAD), depression, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) presented with a cat bite and subsequent wrist pain, concerning for septic arthritis versus cellulitis.

Upon arrival, the patient's vital signs included temperature 98.6°F, heart rate 59 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98%, blood pressure 154/86 mmHg, and pain rating 10 out of 10. Her chief complaint was cat bite. Initial lab results revealed white blood cell count 8.6 K/μL, glucose 151 mg/dL, and lactic acid 2.1 mmol/L.

An MRI of the wrist was conducted due to concern for septic arthritis; however, the examination was limited and did not provide conclusive evidence of osteomyelitis. Findings included significant soft tissue swelling over the dorsal left wrist extending up to the metacarpophalangeal joints, distinct puncture marks at the level of the distal radius, and probable tenosynovitis of the extensor carpi radialis tendons.

The patient was initially administered unasyn in the emergency department and transferred to medicine for further management. During her stay, she was given ampicillin/sulbactam, received a tetanus vaccine, and remained comfortable while lying in bed with her left arm wrapped and in a splint. Upon discharge, her vitals stabilized with a slight decrease in blood pressure (142/50 mmHg). The patient was sent home with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, acetaminophen, aspirin, atorvastatin, clopidogrel, ranitidine, sertraline, and glyburide.

The final diagnosis was cellulitis, with secondary diagnoses including diabetes, CAD, depression, and GERD. The patient's mental status, activity status, and level of consciousness improved throughout her hospital course, though she remained confused at times.</s>

On __, Mr. __ was admitted via ambulance with chief complaints of chest pain. A multidetector helical CT scan of the chest revealed a Type A aortic dissection originating at the aortic root, extending throughout the aortic arch, descending aorta, and into the abdomen. The dissection involved multiple branches including the left main coronary artery, brachiocephalic artery, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries. The inferior extent of the dissection was not fully evaluated, but it extended to at least the superior mesenteric artery and possibly the iliac arteries.

Upon arrival, the patient underwent an emergency Bentall procedure with a 21-mm composite valve graft, replacement of the ascending aorta and hemiarch, and coronary button reimplantation. Post-operatively, the patient experienced atrial fibrillation, which was treated with Amiodarone.

By post-operative day one, the patient was extubated and tolerated beta-blockade. Chest tubes were removed, and the patient was transferred to the surgical stepdown unit. Amiodarone was discontinued due to the patient's history of thyroid dysfunction, and the patient remained in a sinus rhythm. The epicardial wires were removed on post-operative day three. The patient continued physical therapy and was diuresed towards their preoperative weight.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of Type A aortic dissection, post-repair, and post-operative atrial fibrillation. The discharge medications included aspirin, oxycodone-acetaminophen, amiodarone, acetaminophen, simvastatin, warfarin, metoprolol tartrate, and lisinopril. The patient was advised to follow up with their attending physician.</s>

On __, the patient, a female, presented to the Emergency Department reporting chronic pelvic and abdominal pain, accompanied by vaginal bleeding and daily use of multiple tampons and pads due to heavy bleeding. The patient reported a recent episode of nausea/vomiting. Upon examination, the temperature was 97.3°F, heart rate 104 bpm, respiration rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99%, blood pressure 140/79 mmHg, pain score 10, and acuity 3.0.

Upon admission, a pelvic ultrasound revealed a multifibroid uterus, with several fibroids, some having a submucosal component. The largest fibroid measured approximately 5 x 4.6 x 3.7 cm, with central areas of degeneration. A left adnexal hydrosalpinx was also observed, appearing complex with potential for infection. Bilateral dilated fallopian tubes with complex contents were detected, with less than expected wall hyperenhancement compared to what would be expected for pyosalpinges.

Pain control was achieved using IV and oral medications such as hydromorphone, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and docusate sodium. Antibiotic treatment was initiated with doxycycline hyclate, administered twice daily starting on the day of sonohysterogram.

An MRI indicated a 3.9 cm intracavitary fibroid with varying degrees of degeneration. The patient underwent an EUA and US-guided IUD removal. Laboratory tests showed slight increases in white blood cell count, but no other significant findings. The final diagnosis was degenerating uterine fibroids and menorrhagia. At discharge, the patient was sent home with prescriptions for medroxyprogesterone acetate, hydrocodone, ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and docusate sodium, with instructions to continue doxycycline hyclate for a specified duration.</s>

In addition to the imaging results, we observed that you have a history of chronic conditions such as high blood pressure, hepatitis C, and diabetes, among others. As you return home, keep an eye on your symptoms and monitor for any new developments regarding your digestive system. If you notice persistent abdominal pain, dark stools, or other unusual symptoms, please consult your healthcare provider immediately.

Regarding your ongoing dialysis, ensure you maintain your current dialysis schedule as advised by your nephrologist. Continue taking your regular medications as prescribed, paying particular attention to those added during your recent hospital stay.

Dear Patient,

You were recently admitted to our facility due to a fall, leading to a laceration on your left hand. During your stay, several tests were conducted including a CT Head Without Contrast, a CT Spine Without Contrast, and an MRI and MRA Brain Without Contrast.

From the CT Head Without Contrast, it appears there is a 8 mm focus of hyperattenuation in the right frontal lobe periventricular white matter, adjacent to the frontal horn of the right lateral ventricle. This finding could indicate a small intraparenchymal hemorrhage, cavernoma, or another mass lesion. However, further assessment with brain MRI with contrast is recommended for more detailed analysis.

The CT Spine Without Contrast revealed minor issues, including widening of the intervertebral disc space anteriorly at C4-C5, associated with an anterior disc bulge but no prevertebral soft tissue swelling. Additionally, there is minimal anterolisthesis of C5 on C6, C6 on C7, and C7 on T1, potentially indicating chronic degenerative changes. It is advised to consult a specialist regarding potential concerns about ligamentous injuries.

The MRI and MRA Brain Without Contrast showed various findings. Firstly, severely motion degraded MP RAGE sequences, which are essentially non-diagnostic. Secondly, no evidence for acute infarction. Thirdly, an 8 mm right frontal lobe white matter lesion demonstrating extensive blooming on gradient echo sequences, most compatible with a small cavernoma. Fourthly, curvilinear areas of susceptibility artifact with increased FLAIR signal abnormality and ex vacuo dilatation of the right occipital lobe and horn, possibly representing chronic infarction with encephalomalacia and old hemorrhagic products. Lastly, global parenchymal volume loss, evidence of chronic small vessel ischemic disease, and paranasal sinus disease were observed.

Regarding treatment, you did not undergo any surgeries or invasive procedures during your stay. Upon discharge, you should continue taking Omeprazole 20mg daily, as prescribed before admission.

Follow-up appointments are necessary to monitor your health status. Please schedule visits with your attending neurologist and primary care physician as soon as possible.

Should you experience any of the following symptoms – sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth, sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to you, sudden weakness of one side of the body, sudden drooping of one side of the face, or sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body – please seek emergency medical attention immediately by dialing 911.

Take good care of yourself, and we hope for a speedy recovery!

Best regards,
Your Neurology Team</s>

We appreciate your stay with us at our facility. During your admission, you were diagnosed with Cellulitis of the Face. To manage this condition, we performed a procedure called Incision and Drainage (I&D), and initiated treatment with temporary-sulfamethoxazole. Upon further examination, it was decided to switch to Vancomycin and Amp-Sulbactam due to the presence of Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) in your preliminary wound culture. We also conducted a CT Scan of your Sinus, Mandible, and Maxillofacial areas, which showed some degree of soft tissue edema consistent with cellulitis. Your lab results throughout your stay showed improving white blood cell count and lactic acid levels.

As part of your ongoing treatment, please take the following medications as directed:
- Vancomycin
- Amp-Sulbactam
- Ibuprofen (for pain relief)
- Adderall (to manage ADHD)

Remember to attend these upcoming appointments:
1. Follow-up appointment with your primary care physician in one week.
2. Specialty appointment with a dermatologist in two weeks.

If you notice any worsening or new symptoms related to your face or overall health, please seek immediate medical attention. It is essential to maintain good hydration while recovering at home, especially considering your initial low kidney function.

Take care and best wishes for a speedy recovery!

Your ___ Care Team</s>
column3: __ is a __ year old female admitted with right facial cellulitis. Initially presenting with a small red bump on the right cheek that rapidly increased in size with associated edema and pain, she was initially treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. However, the swelling persisted and she developed severe facial swelling, difficulty moving the right mouth, and intra-oral bulging on the right cheek. Upon presentation to the ED, vital signs were T 98.2 HR 62 BP 124/70 RR 14 O2 100%, with lab results significant for WBC 11.3, platelets 123, and lactic acid 3.4. A CT scan showed soft tissue edema consistent with cellulitis and a small non-drainable abscess. She was started on Vancomycin and Amp-Sulbactam upon transfer to the hospital, and observed overnight in the ED. Her condition stabilized, with repeat labs showing WBC 7.8, H/H 11.5/34.9, platelets 122, and lactic acid 0.8. Due to the extent of the infection, she was admitted to Medicine. During her stay, a wound culture revealed methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. She remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable throughout her hospitalization. Prior to discharge, she was switched to amoxicillin, ibuprofen, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, and continued on Adderall. She was discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of right facial cellulitis.</s>

Dear [Patient],

Thank you for entrusting us with your care during your stay at our facility. Here's what happened during your hospital course:

Clinical Events & Findings:
- Upon arrival, you experienced high levels of certain liver enzymes (elevated LFTs) and lipase.
- A CT scan revealed moderate intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation, as well as dilatation of the pancreatic duct.
- During the CT scan, a small irregular hypoattenuating lesion was found at the segment ___ junction, possibly representing a biliary hamartoma. However, no other focal liver lesion was detected.
- The pancreatic parenchyma appeared normal, although there was dilatation of the pancreatic duct to 7mm. No discrete pancreatic mass or abnormal enhancement was identified.
- A biliary stent was placed due to the presence of a biliary stricture, likely caused by an intra-ampullary mass. Multiple large capacity cold forceps biopsies were also taken for histology of the ampullary mass.
- A prominent medial pancreatic head artery from the celiac axis was observed, which may have implications for future treatment planning.

Intervention & Procedures:
- Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP): This procedure allowed for cannulation of the biliary duct, sphincterotomy, and placement of a biliary stent. Cytology samples were also collected for histological analysis.

As you prepare to go home, please remember these key points:

Self-Care Instructions:
- Monitor your liver function tests regularly as advised by your healthcare provider.
- Watch out for any new or unusual symptoms related to your condition, such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or jaundice. If you notice anything concerning, contact your doctor immediately.
- Continue taking your prescribed medications: Timolol Maleate 0.5% 1 drop in each eye twice daily and Cetirizine 10mg once daily at bedtime.
- Attend scheduled follow-up appointments with your specialist(s), including the surgical and medical oncology teams, as directed.

We hope you recover quickly and smoothly at home. Should you have any questions or concerns, don’t hesitate to reach out to us or your primary care physician.

Best regards,
[Facility] Team</s>

The patient, a male with no significant past medical history, presented with abnormal lab values including elevated LFTs and lipase. Upon examination, the liver was found to have moderate intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation with a small hypoattenuating lesion at the segment ___ junction. Notably, the common bile duct was dilated to 14mm, accompanied by pancreatic duct dilatation.

Initially, the patient underwent a CT scan which revealed these findings, colloquially known as the "double duct sign," raising concerns for a pancreatic head or ampullary neoplasm. However, no definitive lesion was observed. Subsequently, an ERCP was conducted, revealing a 2cm mass in the major papilla deemed unresectable. A sphincterotomy was performed in the 12 o'clock position using a sphincterotome over an existing guidewire, exposing the intra-ampullary mass. A 5cm biliary stent was placed successfully, and multiple large capacity cold forceps biopsies were taken for histology. The patient's LFTs and lipase levels fluctuated throughout the hospital stay.

At the time of discharge, the patient's mental status, consciousness level, and activity status were reported as clear and coherent, alert and interactive, and ambulatory – independent respectively. The patient was diagnosed with Ampullary Mass and Bile Duct Obstruction. Further evaluation and management would be required as an outpatient.</s>

The patient, a 65-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, and benign prostatic hypertrophy, presented with right leg cellulitis and an ulceration on the third toe. Upon arrival, vitals included a temperature of 97.2°F, heartrate of 70 bpm, resprate of 20 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation of 100%, systolic blood pressure of 125 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg, and pain rating of 0. The chief complaint was right leg cellulitis.

Initial imaging revealed postsurgical changes at multiple sites, including the right first and fifth metatarsophalangeal joints. Soft tissue induration was observed along the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, though no specific site of cortical destruction or other osseous changes suggesting osteomyelitis were found. The lungs appeared clear, and the heart showed post-CABG changes.

An ulcer excision and closure were performed on the right third toe. Following the procedure, the patient experienced minimal improvement in the cellulitis, with persistent edema and mild erythema. The patient's vital signs remained stable throughout the hospital stay, and there were no reports of fever or increased pain. The patient was able to ambulate independently.

The microbiology culture grew beta streptococcus group G, and the patient was treated with ciprofloxacin and clindamycin. The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of right lower extremity cellulitis and prescriptions for aspirin, atorvastatin, ciprofloxacin, cyanocobalamin, dabigatran etexilate, finasteride, fish oil, lisinopril, metformin, metoprolol succinate extended release, omega-3 fatty acids, oxycodone-acetaminophen, and vitamin D. The patient was advised to follow up as needed.</s>

Despite these interventions, the patient's persistent pain remained a significant issue. It should be noted that the patient has a history of opiate dependency. The patient was deemed fit for discharge to home with close follow-up arrangements.</s>

Urinary Tract Infection and Pulmonary Edema. Upon arrival via ambulance, the patient presented with chief complaints of abdominal pain and altered mental status. Initial lab results revealed hyponatremia (Na 127) and leukocytosis (WBC 7.6). A urine culture later confirmed the presence of Klebsiella pneumoniae. A chest X-ray indicated signs suggestive of decompensated cardiac failure, including new bilateral pleural effusion, widening of the mediastinal vascular pedicle, and worsened cardiomegaly.

Intervention included administration of vancomycin for suspected UTI and treatment of hyponatremia with fluids and electrolytes. Over the course of the admission, the patient's mental status improved, and she became more alert and oriented. However, her vital signs remained somewhat unstable, with a heart rate of 90 bpm and respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute.

An echocardiogram was conducted, which revealed normal global and regional biventricular systolic function, mild aortic regurgitation, and mild pulmonary hypertension. The patient was ultimately discharged to extended care with a diagnosis of urinary tract infection, hyponatremia, and pulmonary edema.</s>

4. **Follow-ups:** Schedule a follow-up appointment with your primary care physician and surgeon as recommended by your attending physician.

5. **Dietary Considerations:** Resume your usual diet gradually, starting with lighter meals and slowly increasing fiber content. Monitor your bowel movements closely and consult your healthcare provider if you experience persistent constipation or diarrhea.

6. **Monitor Symptoms:** Watch for any unusual symptoms like fever, excessive vomiting, or sudden changes in your condition. Immediately seek medical attention if you encounter any concerning symptoms.

We hope you have a smooth recovery. Should you have any concerns or questions, please reach out to us at [contact number].

[Clinic/Hospital Name]</s>
column3: The patient, a ____ year old male, was admitted via ambulance due to a chief complaint of Small Bowel Obstruction (SBO), transfer. Upon arrival, the patient reported abdominal pain and a history of Crohn's disease with multiple ileal resections. A CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed a distal small bowel obstruction centered in the right lower quadrant near the surgical anastomosis with fecalized small bowel loops. During the hospital course, the patient experienced some relief after receiving 4mg morphine and 1mg IV dilaudid in the Emergency Room. His physical examination showed comfort, normal vital signs, and no significant abnormalities. Laboratory results included a slightly elevated white blood cell count (WBC: 4.7) and a moderately increased CRP level (CRP: 4.7). The patient did not require any invasive procedures or surgeries. On the day of discharge, the patient was alert, oriented, ambulatory, and passing semisolid stool. The patient was discharged home with ongoing management of his Crohn's disease and prescribed Ustekinumab injections, Budesonide, Lidocaine-Prilocaine, and Ondansetron for symptom relief.</s>

Dear [Patient],

You have been discharged from our facility following your recent stay due to concerns related to headaches, neck pain, and vertigo. During your hospitalization, we conducted various diagnostic tests including Brain MRI Without Contrast, Brain MRA Without Contrast, Neck MRA With/Without Contrast, Indication: Headaches, neck pain, vertigo, and Comparison: Non-contrast head CT performed earlier on the same day.

Here is a brief summary of your hospital course:

* Diagnostic Tests: Various imaging tests were carried out to evaluate potential causes of your symptoms. These included Brain MRI, Brain MRA, and Neck MRA. The results indicated the presence of a 1.7 x 0.9 cm extra-axial mass adjacent to the right frontal operculum, which is consistent with a meningioma. Additionally, there was mild stenosis at the origin of the left vertebral artery.
* Treatment: While no immediate treatment was necessary during your stay, it was suggested that you consider a follow-up appointment within 12 months, ideally with intravenous contrast, to monitor the meningioma's stability.
* Management Plan: Given the diagnosis of meningioma, it is essential to maintain regular communication with your healthcare team to discuss ongoing management strategies. Your primary care physician can help coordinate follow-ups with specialists as needed.

As you recover at home, please remember to:

* Contact your healthcare provider if you experience any new or worsening symptoms related to your condition.
* Attend scheduled follow-up appointments with your doctors to ensure proper monitoring and management of your health.
* Take any prescribed medication as instructed by your healthcare providers.
* Maintain a healthy lifestyle, including eating a balanced diet, getting regular exercise, and managing stress levels.

Thank you for entrusting us with your care during your stay. We wish you a speedy recovery and hope to see you again soon. Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you have any questions or concerns.

Best regards,
[Clinician]</s>
column3: The patient was admitted to the neurosurgery service due to complaints of severe headaches. Initial lab work showed a white blood cell count of 6.5 with 93.8% neutrophils, glucose of 188, lactate of 1.6, negative urine analysis, and negative flu swab. Chest X-ray showed no acute processes. Given the absence of a clear source of infection, they decided to hold antibiotics and believed the process to be most likely viral in nature. The patient received intravenous fluids, acetaminophen, and was started back on her home medications/immunosuppressives.

#### Overnight observation and subsequent admission:
Despite initial improvements, the patient remained symptomatic the next morning. She was admitted to the medicine service under Dr. ___. Review of systems included (+) headache, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, myalgia/arthralgia, fever/chills, and (-) rash, cough/dyspnea, dysuria. Physical examination revealed no significant findings.

#### Discharge:
After several days of observation and treatment, the patient's symptoms gradually resolved. She was discharged home with a diagnosis of viral gastroenteritis and acute febrile illness. The patient was advised to continue her current medications including insulin, cyclosporene, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, sulfameth/trimethoprim, tamoxifen citrate, calcium carbonate, vitamin D, lubiprostone, acetaminophen, atorvastatin, and lubiprostone. ### Brief Hospital Course

#### Initial Presentation

The patient, a 57-year-old female, presented with complaints of dyspnea and right leg swelling. Upon arrival, vital signs included temperature 96.9°F, heartrate 92.0 bpm, resprate 18.0 bpm, o2sat 100.0%, sbp 117.0 mmHg, dbp 62.0 mmHg, and pain score 0. The chief complaint was dyspnea and right leg swelling.

#### Investigations and Findings

An initial portable AP chest radiograph revealed mild cardiomegaly, smoothly marginated opacity within the mid to lower left lung consistent with a known loculated effusion, dense left basilar atelectasis, no evidence of pneumothorax, and diffuse bilateral parenchymal nodularity. A subsequent chest (portable AP) showed slight interval increase in ill-defined opacities at the right lung base.

A CT chest with contrast identified stable bilateral pulmonary nodules and pleural nodularity consistent with metastatic disease, persistent loculated left pleural effusion, and no evidence of pulmonary embolism or aortic abnormality. Additionally, there appeared to be interval increase in ill-defined opacities at the right lung base.

A chest ultrasound did not demonstrate significant increase in the patient's prior pleural effusions.

#### Interventions and Treatment

No invasive procedures were performed during this admission. The patient was managed conservatively with oxygen supplementation and diuretics.

#### Progress During Admission

Despite treatment, the patient continued to experience dyspnea and developed mild chest pain related to her prior chest tube sites. There were no reported fevers or chills. Bedside thoracic ultrasound did not reveal significant increases in her prior pleural effusions.

#### Discharge Summary

The patient was discharged with prescriptions for guaifenesin, ipratropium-albuterol nebulizer solution, lorazepam, oxycodone sustained release, simethicone, and acetaminophen. The primary diagnosis was acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, secondary to metastatic pancreatic cancer. The patient was discharged in a stable mental state, able to walk with assistance or aid, and scheduled for follow-up appointments as necessary.</s>

The patient was admitted to the medicine service for management of CHF exacerbation. Notably, the patient experienced a transient episode of hypotension upon arrival, requiring fluid resuscitation with intravenous dextrose (1 amp D50).

Throughout the hospital course, the patient reported increasing shortness of breath, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. These symptoms persisted despite treatment adjustments, including initiation of additional loop diuretics (torsemide and metolazone). Additionally, the patient received a trial of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy for suspected OSA, although it remains uncertain whether this intervention significantly improved his symptoms.

On the final day of hospitalization, the patient's vitals stabilized, and he was deemed ready for discharge. At the time of discharge, the patient's medication regimen consisted primarily of oral antihypertensives, antiplatelet agents, lipid-lowering drugs, and glucose-regulating medications. It should be emphasized that the patient's insulin dosages may require close monitoring and adjustment based on ongoing glucose trends.</s>

Dear [Patient],

Thank you for entrusting us with your care during your recent stay. Here are some guidelines to assist you in your recovery after being treated for a Urinary Tract Infection, recurrent UTIs, and a urethral diverticulum.

1. Continue taking your current medications as directed, except for vancomycin and erythromycin base which you are allergic to. If you have any questions about your medications or their dosages, please consult your primary care physician.

2. Monitor your symptoms closely and contact your healthcare provider immediately if you notice worsening abdominal pain, increased vaginal bleeding, fever, or persistent nausea.

3. Drink plenty of fluids daily to maintain proper hydration levels, especially water and clear liquids.

4. Avoid constipating foods such as dairy, meat, eggs, and processed grains for several days to prevent exacerbating existing digestive issues.

5. Resuming regular physical activity is encouraged; however, avoid heavy lifting or strenuous exercise until cleared by your healthcare provider.

6. It has been confirmed that you had a fibroid detected in your uterus. Your gynecologist will provide more specific guidance regarding this finding.

7. Be aware that you have surgical clips present from a prior cholecystectomy procedure.

We hope you find these instructions helpful in managing your condition moving forward. We wish you a speedy recovery!

Best regards,
[Clinician]</s>
column3: Urinary Tract Infection and Urethral Diverticulum: A 50-year-old female presented with right flank pain, hematuria, and recurrent UTIs. Initial workup included a renal US which revealed no hydronephrosis, stones, or masses; however, a 3cm urethral diverticulum was noted. Subsequent pelvic US confirmed a fibroid uterus with normal ovaries. Upon improvement, she was discharged home with ongoing management of diabetes, depression, hypertension, GERD, obesity, recurrent UTIs, chronic back pain, and fibroid uterus.</s>

Dear [Patient's Name],

Thank you for entrusting us with your care during your recent hospital stay at __. Your admission was due to a head injury sustained from being struck by a football, resulting in symptoms including headaches, seizures, and temporary cognitive impairment.

While under our care, we performed various tests, including a CT scan of your head and a chest X-ray. These scans showed no signs of bleeding, edema, or acute hemorrhage within your brain. However, they did reveal a stable area of hypodensity in the right parietal lobe, which is consistent with previous encephalomalacia. There were no abnormalities found in your lungs or heart.

During your stay, you received transfusions of two units of packed red blood cells. It is essential that you continue to manage your sickle cell disease according to your healthcare providers’ advice, particularly monitoring for potential complications like acute chest syndrome.

As part of your treatment plan, we will adjust your medication regimen as follows:

1. Continue Gabapentin 900mg twice daily for seizure control.
2. Take Hydroxyurea 500mg three times daily to help manage your sickle cell anemia.
3. Resume Oxycodone immediate release as needed for sickle cell crises.
4. Continue Sertraline 100mg twice daily for depression management.

For ongoing symptom relief, please use Acetaminophen 1000mg every 8 hours as needed for pain.

In order to ensure proper management of your conditions, it is crucial that you schedule follow-ups with your neurology team and primary care physician. Specifically, please arrange visits as follows:

- Neurology Follow-Up: To be scheduled with your attending neurologist.
- Primary Care Physician Follow-Up: On [date] at [time].

Lastly, given your history of seizures, please adhere to the following precautions:

- Avoid activities that could potentially cause another seizure, such as driving, operating heavy machinery, climbing ladders, taking baths or swimming unsupervised.
- If you experience additional seizures, contact your healthcare provider immediately.

We hope you recover quickly and wish you continued good health. Should you have any questions or concerns, do not hesitate to reach out to your healthcare team.

Best regards,
[Clinic / Hospital Name]</s>
column3:

On admission, vital signs included temperature 99.2°F, heart rate 68 bpm, respiratory rate 18 bpm, oxygen saturation 99%, systolic blood pressure 126 mmHg, and diastolic blood pressure 62 mmHg. A CT scan of the head without contrast was performed due to a reported head injury and active seizures, revealing no acute intracranial processes, including hemorrhage, edema, or mass effect. A subsequent chest X-ray found no acute cardiopulmonary issues.

Upon neurological examination, the patient exhibited normal mental status, cranial nerve function, motor function, sensory responses, deep tendon reflexes, coordination, and gait. During hospitalization, the patient received two units of packed red blood cells for management of anemia related to sickle cell disease. The patient's chief complaint involved bilateral hand twitching, which persisted despite treatment with gabapentin 900 mg BID and vigabatrin 200 mg BID for seizure control. Additionally, the patient suffered from daily headaches, knee pain, and occasional urinary incontinence.

At discharge, the patient was diagnosed with sickle cell anemia, migraine headache, and seizure disorder. column2:
Dear Mr./Ms.,

We appreciate your stay at our facility and hope this letter finds you recovering well. During your hospitalization, you were diagnosed with Neuromyelitis Optica (Devic). Your course included several interventions and evaluations:

1. MRI of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine showed multiple small foci of T2 hyperintensity extending from C2 to T1, with no postcontrast enhancement. These findings are consistent with demyelination/NMO clinically.
2. Blood tests were conducted, including serum aquaporin-4 (aka NMO) antibodies, which came back negative.
3. Three rounds of plasmapheresis were administered to treat an exacerbation of NMO restricted to the cord.
4. You were started on Mycophenolate Mofetil 1000mg twice daily to continue managing your NMO.

As part of ongoing management, we recommend the following:

1. Continue taking Mycophenolate Mofetil 1000mg twice daily.
2. Begin taking Tizanidine 2 mg PO BID: PRN for persistent back pain.
3. Follow up with your neurologist as needed for monitoring and adjustment of medication regimen.

If you experience any unusual symptoms or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact us or seek medical attention immediately. We wish you a speedy recovery and look forward to seeing you again soon.

Best regards,
[Hospital/Clinic Name] Neurology Team</s>
column3: Ms. __ was admitted to __ due to worsening back pain and numbness, a recurrence of symptoms from previous Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO) episodes. Initial MRI spine revealed stable exam, foci of cervicomedullary junction and cervical cord T2 signal abnormality consistent with demyelination/NMO clinically, diffuse mild cord atrophy, stable anterior foramina magnum meningioma, and degenerative changes. During hospitalization, she received three rounds of plasma exchange (PLEX), with serum Aquaporin-4 (aka NMO) antibodies returning negative. Despite completing additional PLEX sessions as an outpatient, persistent numbness persisted along with new back pain. On examination, she displayed normal mental status, intact cranial nerves, normal motor function, symmetrical decreased sensation to pinprick in right lower back and right lower limb distribution, and normal deep tendon reflexes. Following stabilization, she was discharged home on Tizanidine 2 mg PO BID PRN for back pain and Mycophenolate Mofetil 1000 mg PO BID for management of NMO.</s>

[Clinic/Hospital] Team</s>

column3: ____ m/66 yrs with history of atrial fibrillation, bradycardia, stroke, hypertension, high cholesterol underwent urological admission due to fever and dysuria following prostate biopsy. You were admitted to our hospital with difficulty breathing (shortness of breath) and an abnormal Electrocardiogram (EKG). During your stay, a procedure known as thoracentesis was performed to remove excess fluid from your right pleural cavity. This helped improve your condition.

While in the hospital, imaging tests such as X-rays and Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) of your chest were conducted. These revealed a large non-hemorrhagic right pleural effusion with accompanying atelectasis, indicating buildup of fluid between the layers of your lungs. The right upper lobe of your lung also showed some consolidation, possibly due to pneumonia or re-expansion pulmonary edema. Further testing is needed to confirm the exact cause.

Additionally, a small pneumothorax (air collection in the pleural space) was detected in your right lung. It is essential to monitor this closely.

Before leaving the hospital, please schedule a follow-up appointment with the Interventional Pulmonary Clinic for further investigation into the cause of your pleural effusion. The specific date and time for your appointment will be communicated separately.

As part of your treatment plan, you will need to continue taking medication prescribed by your doctor. Make sure to take them exactly as directed and do not stop unless instructed otherwise.

To help manage your symptoms and promote healing, consider the following tips:

1. Rest as much as possible to allow your body to recover.
2. Avoid activities that strain your chest muscles or increase your breathing rate.
3. Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids.
4. Monitor your temperature regularly and seek medical attention if it exceeds 100°F (38°C).
5. Keep track of any changes in your symptoms and inform your healthcare provider promptly.</s>
column3:
Ms. __ is a female patient who presented with chief complaint of dyspnea, abnormal EKG, and concern for PE. Upon arrival, she exhibited temperature 100.1°F, heartrate 102.0 bpm, resprate 18.0 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation 98.0%, and pain score 0. She was classified as moderately acute.

Initial imaging revealed a large right pleural effusion with accompanying compressive atelectasis, raising concerns for parapneumonic effusion, hemothorax, or malignant effusion. Subsequent thoracentesis was performed to investigate the cause of the unilateral effusion. Analysis of the collected fluid did not reveal any specific etiology.

Following thoracentesis, the patient experienced improvement in her right pleural effusion and consolidation in the right upper lobe, possibly indicating pneumonia. Additional imaging was conducted to evaluate the lung parenchyma and pleural effusion, revealing a small right apical pneumothorax that subsequently decreased in size.

On the final day of hospitalization, another CT abdomen and pelvis exam was ordered to evaluate potential masses in the liver, pancreas, colon, and stomach. No obvious mass lesion was identified in the abdomen or pelvis. The patient was ultimately diagnosed with pneumonia in the inferior right upper lobe, and no additional intrathoracic malignancies were detected.

Ms. __ was discharged with a recommendation for correlation with liver function tests and continued monitoring of her pulmonary condition.</s>

column3:

column3:
### Dizziness Episode

##### Initial Evaluation

This __ y/o F with a medical history of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), renal transplant, and prior Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT), presented with complaints of dizziness. Upon initial examination, vital signs were within normal limits except for an elevated D-dimer. Due to a contrast allergy, a Bedside Lower Extremity Ultrasound (BLE US) was conducted to rule out potential DVT.

##### Ultrasound Findings

The ultrasound revealed normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation in the bilateral common femoral, femoral, and popliteal veins. There was also no evidence of deep venous thrombosis in either lower extremity.

##### Subsequent Events

In the Emergency Department (ED), the patient received multiple medications for symptom relief, including Lorazepam, Mirtazapine, Prazosin, Ziprasidone, Acyclovir, Hydroxychloroquine, Metoprolol, Prednisone, Tacrolimus, and additional medications. Despite these interventions, the patient reported persistent lightheadedness and mental fogginess upon transfer to the medicine unit. On arrival, there was also mild calf tenderness on the right side and rib pain with coughing or deep breathing.

##### Further Investigations

Additional laboratory tests were ordered, which included complete blood count, glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, troponin T, and D-dimer. The results of these tests were not specified in the discharge summary.

##### Progress During Admission

Over the course of hospitalization, the patient's vital signs remained mostly stable, with slight variations in temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate. Physical examination throughout the admission period indicated no abnormalities, apart from mild calf tenderness on the right side.

##### Discharge Summary

At the time of discharge, the patient felt somewhat improved but still experienced lingering lightheadedness and mental fogginess. The cause of these symptoms remains undetermined based on the information provided in the discharge summary. The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of dizziness, and the prescribed medications included Acyclovir, Clindamycin, Epinephrine, Hydroxychloroquine, Lorazepam, Metoprolol, Mirtazapine, Prazosin, Prednisone, Tacrolimus, and Vitamin D.</s>

During hospitalization, he remained asymptomatic regarding pain, nausea, vomiting, and continued to pass flatus. He did not experience any recent weight gain or weight loss, fevers, chills, or night sweats.

The patient was treated with antibiotics, specifically Ciprofloxacin HCl 500mg PO Q12H for 7 days and metronidazole 500mg PO TID for another 7 days. He was discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of right colon perforation.</s>

column3:
This is a __ year old male with past medical history of esophageal disease, GERD, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and varicose veins, who presented with persistent cough and fever despite finishing a Z-pack. Upon arrival, vital signs included temperature 98.4°F, heartrate 89 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95%, systolic blood pressure 107 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure 58 mmHg, and pain score 6/10. The chief complaint was cough, syncope, weakness, dyspnea on exertion, dizziness.

On initial evaluation, a CXR revealed bilateral pneumonia and suspected interstitial lung disease. Subsequent CTA chest confirmed these findings, revealing bilateral ground-glass opacities with subpleural reticulation, reticular opacities, and thickening of bronchovascular bundles, most suggestive of a fibrotic subtype nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP). Medications prescribed at discharge include clobetasol propionate cream, doxazosin, finasteride, a mucous membrane solution for pain relief, levofloxacin, and a prescription for the latter medication (Levaquin). At discharge, the patient was alert and interactive, ambulating independently, and clear in thought processes. Follow-up appointments were recommended.</s>

During your hospitalization, additional imaging was performed to evaluate the progression of the obstruction. Although the obstruction persisted, there was slight improvement observed in the degree of small bowel dilation compared to earlier images. Additionally, oral contrast has passed into the colon, indicating potential resolution of the obstruction.

Overnight, the pain intensified, and you experienced episodes of nausea and vomiting. Initially, attempts were made to manage the condition conservatively; however, the pain became unmanageable, prompting your decision to seek further medical attention.

While in the hospital, you remained hemodynamically stable throughout your stay. Your physical examination showed a distended abdomen, but no other significant findings.

As part of your treatment, no major surgical or invasive procedures were necessary. Instead, efforts focused on managing your symptoms through supportive measures.

Here are some guidelines for your post-discharge period:

* Activity: Avoid heavy lifting or straining for the first week after discharge. Gradually return to normal activities as tolerated.
* Diet: Begin with a low-fiber diet initially and gradually advance to a regular diet as tolerated.
* Pain Management: Take prescribed pain medication as directed. Contact your healthcare provider if pain becomes severe or persists beyond the expected duration.
* Bowel Function: Monitor your bowel habits closely. Passing small amounts of dark, old-looking stools and occasional bright red blood in the stool is expected. However, if you notice prolonged constipation, bright red blood with bowel movements, or loose stool without improvement, please contact your healthcare provider.
* Follow-Up Care: Schedule a follow-up appointment with your primary care physician or gastroenterologist as advised by your attending physician.</s>
column3:

The left common femoral vein showed a nonocclusive clot with some residual color flow, while the left proximal femoral, mid femoral, and distal femoral veins were partially compressible with transducer pressure. The left popliteal vein was also distended with echogenic contents, noncompressible with transducer pressure, and lacking flow on color or spectral Doppler. No color flow was demonstrated in the left peroneal and posterior tibial veins. These findings suggest acute DVT in all imaged bilateral deep veins, with the left common femoral, proximal femoral, and mid femoral being partially occlusive with minimal residual flow.

In light of these findings, an inferior vena cava filter was inserted as a major invasive procedure. During the hospital stay, the patient felt well with no specific complaints, denying pain in her legs. Her INR results were unavailable in the provided discharge report.</s>

# NEUROLOGY - Shaking Episode

Patient __, a right-handed male, presented with a sudden onset of rhythmic jerking involving the right hemibody, including the arm, leg, face, and associated symptoms such as difficulty speaking, swallowing, and blurred vision. These symptoms significantly improved after administration of Ativan.

Upon admission, a comprehensive neurological examination was conducted, revealing no abnormalities in mental status, cranial nerves, motor function, sensory perception, coordination, or gait. Notably, there were no signs of asterixis, intention tremor, or dysdiadochokinesia. Deep tendon reflexes, plantar responses, and crossed adductor responses were within normal limits.

An MRI scan was ordered to investigate potential causes for the patient's symptoms. The results indicated a normal brain MRI with no abnormalities, lesions, or areas of enhancement observed.

With no concerning findings on physical examination and normal imaging results, the attending physician concluded that the shaking episode was likely idiopathic. Given the rapid resolution of symptoms with Ativan and the absence of any red flags, the patient was deemed fit for discharge.

At discharge, the patient was fully alert, oriented, and ambulatory, with a completely intact neurologic exam. No additional medication was prescribed upon discharge, and the patient was advised to return for follow-up should similar episodes occur in the future.</s>

Mr. ___ is a __-year-old male with a past medical history of afib, multiple ischemic and hemorrhagic infarcts, cerebral amyloid angiopathy. He presented with a 2.5-month history of headaches and difficulty writing. On admission, the patient reported gradual onset of headache, initially mild but worsening since, primarily located on the right posterior region but later becoming holocephalic. The headache was associated with photophobia and phonophobia, but no nausea, vomiting, or transient visual obscurations (TVOs). The headache was worst at night and affected his ability to sleep. Prior history included headaches attributed to occipital neuralgia, for which gabapentin was initiated but the patient missed subsequent neurology appointments.

On examination, the patient exhibited mild word-finding difficulties, difficulty spelling and reading, and difficulty remembering the storyline of a television show immediately after its end. He also experienced difficulty ambulating in the house, expressing concerns about tripping over shadows. Noteworthy physical examination findings include dense right hemianopia, subtle left pronation without drift, and full motor strength throughout.

Imaging studies revealed no evidence of acute intracranial hemorrhage, infarction, or mass lesion. However, a focus of increased susceptibility in the left occipital lobe indicated chronic blood products from a remote hemorrhage, while numerous punctate foci of increased susceptibility suggested microhemorrhages. A 2mm posterior-directed outpouching from the left supraclinoid internal carotid artery was noted, potentially representing an infundibulum versus a small aneurysm. Mild-to-moderate narrowing of the left P2 segment and probable V4 segment of the right vertebral artery was observed, along with asymmetric parenchymal atrophy of the posterior left temporal and occipital lobes, indicative of presumed moderate chronic small vessel ischemic changes.

Throughout the hospital course, the patient's headaches persisted despite attempts to manage them with various medications. Upon discharge, the attending recommended continuing current medications, including propranolol, amlodipine, gabapentin, lisinopril, and zolpidem tartrate. The patient was advised to follow up with his primary care provider within a specified period for ongoing management of his blood pressure.</s>

* Keep your incision clean and dry until your sutures or staples are removed. Showering is allowed, but avoid getting water directly on the incision site.

* Contact your surgeon immediately if you notice signs of infection, such as redness, fever, or drainage near the incision site.
* Avoid strenuous activities, such as heavy lifting, running, climbing, or contact sports, until your follow-up appointment. Gradually resume regular activities as advised by your healthcare team.

As part of your treatment, we administered IV Zofran for nausea relief. Upon discharge, you will require ongoing management for your symptoms. Specifically, we recommend outpatient physical therapy for vestibular and gait training.

Upon arrival via ambulance, the patient presented with chief complaints of sore throat, weakness, and nausea. Initial vital signs included temperature 98.2°F, heart rate 129 bpm, respiration rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 100%, blood pressure 139/89 mmHg, and acuity score 2.0.

Computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck revealed no evidence of tonsillar, peritonsillar, or retropharyngeal abscess. However, the tonsils appeared hyperemic, potentially indicating tonsillitis. There was also minor mucosal thickening present in both maxillary sinuses.

Throughout the hospital stay, the patient received treatment primarily focused on managing symptoms associated with streptococcal pharyngitis. Specific interventions included antibiotics such as penicillin G benzathine and azithromycin, analgesics like ibuprofen, and antipsychotics including diphenhydramine hydrochloride. Antihistamines and corticosteroids were also prescribed to alleviate inflammation and reduce swelling.

By the time of discharge, the patient showed noticeable improvement in their sore throat symptoms, although they continued to experience residual weakness and occasional dry cough. Their mental status remained clear and coherent throughout the course of their hospitalization. At discharge, the primary diagnosis was Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis – severe.</s>

The brief hospital course for this patient involved an admission due to altered mental status, characterized by decreased cognition, poor memory, and feeling unwell. Upon initial examination, the patient had a temperature of 98.7°F, heart rate of 85 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 100%, systolic blood pressure of 183 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure of 79 mmHg, and pain score of 2 out of 10.

An extensive workup was conducted, including a CTA head and neck, which revealed a subacute left posterior cerebral artery territory infarction, a short segment dissection of the proximal left V2 segment vertebral artery with associated high-grade luminal stenosis, patent intracranial vasculature, and a partially visualized moderate-sized left pleural effusion. Additionally, a periapical lucency was found at the left maxillary teeth, requiring non-urgent follow-up with dentistry.

A noncontrast head CT and MRI head without contrast were also performed, confirming the presence of the left PCA infarct and revealing white matter and pontine FLAIR hyperintensities, likely sequela of chronic small vessel disease.

Throughout the hospital stay, the patient's symptoms remained stable, and she was ambulating without difficulty prior to her discharge. It should be noted that her A1c was 6.9, and her lipid panel was abnormally elevated. The patient was discharged on several medications, including Amiodarone, Aspirin, Folate, Fluoxetine, Hydrochlorothiazide, Lisinopril, Mirtazapine, Nicotine Patch, Pravastatin, Ranitidine, and Metoprolol Succinate Extended Release.</s>

Dear _,

We are pleased to inform you that you have been discharged from our care following treatment for a seizure episode. Your stay included various tests and interventions to determine the cause of your seizure.

While in the hospital, you received imaging examinations, including a chest X-ray, CT scan of the head without contrast, portable chest X-ray, MRI of the brain with and without contrast, and another portable chest X-ray. These scans helped us evaluate potential issues like bleeding or infections, and they did not reveal any significant concerns regarding those areas. However, we found ongoing changes in your brain associated with previous surgeries, specifically a right craniectomy and right middle cerebral artery aneurysm coiling. Additionally, a small, evolving focus in the right frontal lobe was observed, though its exact nature remains uncertain. Further investigation, possibly involving additional imaging studies, may provide more clarity about this finding.

To manage your seizures going forward, we have adjusted your medication regimen. Specifically, we have changed your anticonvulsants to lacosamide 100 mg twice daily and phenytoin sodium extended 400 mg once daily at bedtime. It's essential that you continue taking these medications exactly as directed. If you have any questions or concerns about your medications, please contact your healthcare provider.

In terms of follow-up care, it would be beneficial for you to schedule appointments with your attending neurologist and primary care physician as indicated below. Regular checkups will help monitor your condition and ensure proper management of your seizures.

Should you experience any of the following symptoms, please seek immediate emergency medical attention by dialing 911:
- Sudden partial or complete loss of vision
- Sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth
- Sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to you
- Sudden weakness of one side of the body
- Sudden drooping of one side of the face
- Sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body

Thank you for entrusting your care to us during your hospital stay. We wish you a speedy recovery and hope for continued good health.

Best regards,
[Your Care Team]</s>

The patient, a male, was initially admitted via ambulance due to a seizure incident. Upon arrival, he was intubated and received ativan for airway protection. During his stay, he experienced another seizure episode while asleep, resolving upon waking.

An extensive workup included a chest X-ray, which revealed a properly positioned endotracheal tube, clear lungs, and minimal linear atelectasis or scar at the left lung base. A CT head scan without contrast showed ongoing postsurgical changes in the right frontal and parietal lobes from a previous right craniectomy and right middle cerebral artery aneurysm coiling. No acute hemorrhage was observed, though a hypodense focus in the right frontal lobe cortex was noted, with uncertainty regarding its chronicity and nature.

Additionally, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was conducted, revealing residual blood products along the surgical bed and right Sylvian fissure, with no evidence of acute or subacute ischemic changes. Encephalomalacia was seen in the right temporal lobe, causing ex vacuo dilation of the right lateral ventricle. No abnormal enhancement was detected to indicate leptomeningeal disease, but there was mild dural enhancement noted along the surgical bed and right Sylvian fissure.

Throughout his hospital stay, the patient's neurological status remained relatively stable, with no significant improvements or deteriorations. He was eventually discharged home with a change in seizure medication regimen, including Lacosamide 100 mg PO BID, Phenytoin Sodium Extended 400 mg PO QHS, and Phenytoin Infatab 50 mg PO QHS.</s>
